title: Paraguay President Impeached Minutes After Resigning Amid Bank Collapse Crisis
body:
Paraguayan legislators moved swiftly to strip President Santiago Peña of his office on Thursday, voting unanimously to impeach him just minutes after he submitted his resignation. The dramatic turn of events follows the sudden collapse of Banco Digital, a state‑linked fintech that left millions of Paraguayans unable to access their savings and ignited a wave of public outrage. Peña’s brief attempt to step down was rendered moot by the lower house’s decision, effectively ending his five‑year tenure and plunging the nation into a constitutional crisis.

The impeachment vote, carried out by the Chamber of Deputies, was unanimous—an unprecedented show of consensus in a country where political divisions have long been entrenched. Lawmakers cited “grave misconduct” and “abuse of public trust” as the grounds for removal, referencing the president’s alleged role in facilitating the bank’s rapid expansion despite warnings from regulators. Peña, who had risen to power on a platform of modernising Paraguay’s financial sector, now faces criminal investigations that could see him barred from holding public office for years.

Banco Digital, launched in 2021 as part of Peña’s “digital transformation” agenda, quickly amassed over 1.2 million account holders, promising higher returns and low fees through a proprietary app. However, the bank’s aggressive lending practices, reliance on volatile cryptocurrency assets, and opaque governance structure left it vulnerable to market shocks. When a sudden devaluation of regional digital currencies hit in early March, the bank’s liquidity evaporated, prompting a freeze on withdrawals that affected an estimated 2.5 billion guaraníes (roughly US$340 million) in customer deposits. The government’s initial assurances that the crisis was “contained” did little to calm a populace already wary of corruption and elite capture.

Political analysts see Peña’s downfall as the culmination of mounting pressure from both opposition parties and civil society. Over the past year, protests have swelled each time the administration pushed through controversial reforms, such as the 2023 tax code overhaul and a controversial land‑use policy that favoured multinational agribusinesses. The bank scandal added fuel to an already volatile mix, exposing how the president’s push for rapid digitalisation may have outpaced institutional capacity and oversight. “What we are witnessing is not just a financial debacle, but a failure of governance that eroded the social contract,” said María López, a professor of political science at the National University of Asunción.

The impeachment also raises questions about the constitutional succession plan. According to Paraguay’s 1992 constitution, the vice president assumes the presidency in the event of a vacancy, but Peña’s resignation and immediate impeachment create a legal gray area. Vice President Luis Mora, a longtime ally of Peña, has so far remained silent, while opposition leader Pedro García has called for a caretaker government to oversee new elections within six months. International observers, including the Organization of American States, have expressed concern over the speed of the proceedings, urging transparency and adherence to due process to maintain regional stability.

Looking ahead, Paraguay faces a dual challenge: restoring confidence in its financial system and navigating a potentially turbulent political transition. The central bank has pledged to conduct a forensic audit of Banco Digital and to establish a compensation fund for affected depositors, though the timeline remains uncertain. Meanwhile, the upcoming legislative session will likely focus on tightening regulatory oversight of fintech ventures and revisiting the legal framework that allowed a single institution to wield such outsized influence. As the nation grapples with the fallout, the impeachment of President Peña may serve as a cautionary tale about the perils of unchecked digital ambition, underscoring the need for robust institutions that can safeguard both the economy and democratic governance.
